title: QR-code phishing (quishing)
body_md:
## A chalk arrow vouches for nothing

Dusk, a drizzle, a parking meter with a glossy sticker on its face: scan to pay from your phone. A QR code is a chalk arrow on the pavement. It points somewhere and promises nothing. The squares can hold a web address or other data, but they won’t tell you who put the arrow there, who runs what it points to, or whether the request behind it is real. QR phishing, sometimes called quishing, lives in that gap. One scan carries you from a sign on a wall, or from a message, into the browser in your pocket, where a fake payment or sign-in page can look perfectly routine.

Setting matters. A printed sticker can cover a venue’s real code. A QR in an unexpected email can carry a supposed password reset off the computer where it arrived and onto your phone. And plenty of honest cafés and ticket desks use QR codes too. So the rule is not “every code is dangerous.” Before you act, check three things: the **task, the placement and the destination**.

### A careful way to scan

1. Ask whether you expected this code and whether the action makes sense where you found it. A code that hurries you into a password reset or a fine is a reason to go another way.
2. At a public payment point, look for a sticker layered over another code, but don’t take neat printing as proof. Ask staff, or use the official parking or payment app you already know.
3. If you do scan, use your phone’s built-in camera or a scanner you trust, and read the destination it shows **before you open it**. How much of the address you see depends on the device and the app. If you can’t read it, don’t guess.
4. On the page that opens, check the address bar again before you enter money or sign-in details. The preview may show a middle step that redirects. HTTPS protects the connection; it doesn’t vouch for whoever is taking the payment.

A QR code in an email about your account can simply be skipped: open the service’s app or site yourself. With a restaurant menu, it is reasonable to ask staff if the code looks pasted over or wants personal details you didn’t expect. Scanning alone is not the same as giving away a password or paying. But if you did enter sign-in or card details, act quickly through the real provider and look over your account.

The codes and addresses in this lesson are invented. Don’t scan real public codes as practice, and don’t type anything into a course exercise.

widget_config.goal: Before acting on a QR code, check where it sits, what it is for and where it leads, and use a route you know for payments and sign-ins.
widget_config.today_action: At a familiar venue, or on a ticket you already have, notice where the QR code is printed. Decide which independent contact or app you would use if it looked tampered with. Do not scan anything for this exercise.
widget_config.scope: Everyday advice for ordinary users. The FTC’s reporting and payment advice applies to the US; device previews and local payment systems differ. All the scenarios are invented.

sources.title: US FTC: QR stickers on parking meters
sources.scope: Reports of stickers over parking-meter codes, and previewing the URL. Published in September 2026; US context.

sources.title: UK NCSC: spotting scam messages
sources.scope: Warns about QR codes in phishing emails and advises contacting the organization separately.

blocks.title: The parking sticker
blocks.situation: At a public meter, a glossy QR sticker is stuck over an older printed code. A sign nearby says you must pay within two minutes, on a new website.
blocks.analysis: A sticker over another code and a two-minute rush are enough to distrust this payment route, and neat printing proves nothing. Use the operator’s known app, another official way to pay, or ask staff. Do not enter a card on the page the code opens.

blocks.title: The café menu
blocks.situation: A café prints a QR code inside its menus. Staff confirm it leads to the menu page. Your phone’s preview shows a short address specific to the venue, and the page asks for no login or payment.
blocks.analysis: Where the code sits and what staff say both support the ordinary explanation, and you can always ask for a paper menu anyway. A code is not dangerous in itself. If the page suddenly asks for an account or a card, stop and ask staff again.

blocks.title: At the museum desk
blocks.setup: An invented exercise. A visitor sees a QR code for a timed-entry ticket. There is no live code to scan.

steps.prompt: A sticker on the entrance sign says “scan to avoid losing your slot.” What do you look at?

choices.text: Scan at once; a deadline sounds official.
choices.consequence: You let the sign choose your payment route before checking anything.
choices.explanation: Urgency does nothing to prove a sticker is genuine.

choices.text: Look for an overlay, and compare it with the ticket or app instructions the museum already gave you.
choices.consequence: You check where the code sits and what it is for before anything else.
choices.explanation: A physical surface can be tampered with.

steps.prompt: The sticker seems to be layered over an older code. What next?

choices.text: Ask the desk staff, or open the ticket you already hold in your app.
choices.consequence: You get a second route to the same task.
choices.explanation: Staff or a known app can clear it up without the sticker.

choices.text: Use it anyway; it is on museum property.
choices.consequence: You mistake a public surface for permission.
choices.explanation: Anyone with access can stick something on a wall.

steps.prompt: Staff say tickets never need a further payment, but the preview shows https://museum-entry-pay.example. What now?

choices.text: Do not open it, and show staff where the sticker is.
choices.consequence: They can inspect it and take it down.
choices.explanation: The preview and the staff’s answer together are reason enough to stop.

choices.text: Open it to see how much it asks.
choices.consequence: You step toward a payment form nobody has confirmed.
choices.explanation: A demand for money contradicts the process staff just confirmed.

steps.prompt: Imagine you had already typed in your card details before you asked anyone. What matters now?

choices.text: Wait until a charge actually appears before doing anything.
choices.consequence: You put off the response to possible card fraud.
choices.explanation: Calling the issuer promptly beats waiting.

choices.text: Contact your card issuer through its app or a number you already know, and review the transactions.
choices.consequence: The issuer can advise on the card and the charges.
choices.explanation: Say exactly what you entered, and follow the issuer’s own procedure.

blocks.debrief: What counted was the changed surface and the museum’s own answer. The preview helped, but a destination alone proved nothing about honesty. Go back to any choice that the sticker’s urgency made for you.

questions.prompt: A workplace email says to scan a QR code to renew your password. What is the safer route?

choices.text: Open the work sign-in portal you normally use, or ask IT through its known channel.
choices.explanation: You can check the task without the code in the email.

choices.text: Scan it; QR images get screened more thoroughly than links.
choices.explanation: The code still holds an address that needs checking.

questions.prompt: A restaurant’s printed menu has a QR code that staff confirmed. What is reasonable?

choices.text: Treat every QR code as proof of fraud.
choices.explanation: Honest codes are common; context decides.

choices.text: Use it or decline it, and stop if it unexpectedly asks for sensitive data.
choices.explanation: Confirmation helps, but what the page asks still matters.

questions.prompt: A scanner shows a plausible first address, then the page redirects to a card form. What must you check?

choices.text: The final address in the browser, and whether the payment request matches a process you know.
choices.explanation: What counts is who receives your details at the moment you enter them.

choices.text: Nothing; the first address looked fine.
choices.explanation: A redirect can change who receives your details.

questions.prompt: You scanned a suspicious code but entered nothing. What follows?

choices.text: That you have definitely lost the account.
choices.explanation: Scanning alone does not mean a password was disclosed.

choices.text: Stop interacting, close the page, and work out whether you entered or downloaded anything.
choices.explanation: What you do next depends on what was actually exposed.
